'Three nights this week past ten,' said Zeenat, dropping onto the sofa in the break room. 'So much for our seven o'clock rule.'
'The release wasn't optional,' said Tanuja. 'If we'd left at seven, it wouldn't have shipped.'
'So the rule is useless?'
'No. It's just too stiff. What if crunch weeks are allowed, but only when a release truly needs it, and the day after is lighter? No meetings, leave on time.'
'And the rest of the month stays seven o'clock?'
'Yes. The rule stays. It just bends for the real peaks.'
'I can live with that,' Zeenat said. They wrote it on the whiteboard: Crunch allowed. Lighter day after. Otherwise seven.
'Better than pretending we'll never work late,' said Tanuja.

qa.q: What did Zeenat and Tanuja write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: They wrote: Crunch allowed. Lighter day after. Otherwise seven.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when dropping onto the sofa?
qa.a: Zeenat felt tired and frustrated, and doubted whether the seven o'clock rule meant anything.

qa.q: What could go wrong with the new rule, and how could they fix it?
qa.a: Every week might get labelled a crunch week, so they could agree what counts as a real release peak and review the rule each month.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team feel about the new rule?
qa.a: They may feel relieved that limits still exist but bend for real peaks, and that a lighter day follows.

grounding: After a release week forces late nights, Tanuja and Zeenat agree that crunch weeks are allowed with a lighter day afterwards.

passage:
When Bhavna and I set up our team's "no work after 7" rule in January, I was proud of it. Then came release week in March. Four nights in a row we were on calls till midnight fixing a payment bug. By Friday I felt like a fraud for breaking our own rule, and Bhavna was snapping at everyone. "Jasleen, this rule is making us miserable," Bhavna said.
The next Monday we sat down with the rule on a sticky note and looked at it properly. The problem wasn't the late nights; releases happen. The problem was pretending they wouldn't. So we rewrote it: in a release week, late nights are allowed, but the day after the release everyone starts at noon and there are no meetings.
We tried it in May. It wasn't perfect, but nobody felt guilty, and the noon start actually happened.

qa.q: How many nights in a row were they on calls during release week?
qa.a: Four nights in a row, till midnight, fixing a payment bug.

qa.q: What does "I felt like a fraud" tell you about Jasleen's feelings?
qa.a: Jasleen felt guilty and ashamed for breaking a rule the pair had made, even though the late nights were needed.

qa.q: What would you change first if the noon start kept getting skipped?
qa.a: Jasleen and Bhavna could block the noon start in everyone's calendar ahead of time and ask the manager to protect it.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see the rewritten rule?
qa.a: The team will likely find it more believable, since it admits releases happen and still promises them a rest afterwards.

grounding: It shows a team noticing their strict evening rule breaking in a release week and revising it to allow peak nights followed by a lighter day.

Team note, after the June release.
Sangeeta and Lavanya have kept a strict "offline at 6.30" rule since spring, and I was glad of it. Then release week came. Both stayed until ten on three nights, and on Thursday Lavanya came to my desk to apologise for "failing the rule".
I asked them to bring the rule to Monday's retro instead of apologising. Sangeeta put it plainly: "The rule works for normal weeks. It breaks on peaks, and then we feel bad twice." They proposed a change: release weeks are named in advance, late work in them is fine, and the day after a release is a light day with no meetings.
I agreed and added it to the team page. In the July release they stayed late twice, then took Friday easy. No apologies this time. I'll check in again after August.

qa.q: What did Lavanya apologise for on Thursday?
qa.a: Lavanya apologised to the note-writer for "failing the rule".

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when apologising for "failing the rule"?
qa.a: Lavanya felt guilty and ashamed, as if the late nights were a personal failure rather than a normal peak.

qa.q: What else could help the team keep the light day after future releases?
qa.a: The note-writer could block the light day in everyone's calendar in advance so meetings don't creep into it.

qa.q: How does the rule change look to Sangeeta?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees it as more honest: it keeps the limit for normal weeks and stops the team feeling bad twice when a peak comes.

grounding: It shows a team reviewing an evening rule after a release week and loosening it so peak weeks allow late work followed by a light day.
